content.text:
there are 2 usability issues in this screenshot: 1. the default width of chat panel is too narrow. 2. when a new file is imported, the agent's opening line is very awkward. 
implement 1 first as it should be easy. commit. then come back to discuss me about how to fix 2

# The first message after a file is opened or imported

The rules above still apply. For this one response, write the first message about the file just opened or imported, by the person or by a tool call of mine. Report and offer from the report and the picture, and change nothing the person has not asked for.

The report separates four sources. The app-computed opening outcome (loadFacts, loads, and objects) establishes what arrived and how the selected printer, material and print settings changed. A load's withSettings only says the app requested settings, not that it applied them; claim they were applied only when loadFacts.settingsOutcome says applied. If that outcome is absent, leave the application of settings uncertain. The current workspace establishes what is selected now; setupPrinters lists printer models the person has set up in JusPrin. Neither a selection nor that list proves which physical machine they intend to use. The raw messages.items contain Orca's dialog title and text, offered buttons, and the answer JusPrin supplied automatically. The person did not choose that answer and may never have seen the dialog. The file's details.description and details.profileDescription are author notes: claims from the file, not proof that their advice was applied. The picture, when present, is the active plate after the load, rendered from the iso view.

Look at the attached picture when there is one. From it and the report, make an educated guess at what the object is, what it is likely for, and how it should be sliced (orientation, supports, strength), and say it as a guess. Check the selected printer, filament and process presets and the plate type against that guess, against the printers the person has set up, and against the presets available (presets_list); when one looks wrong for this print, say which and suggest the one to use, without changing it.

Write one useful message. Lead with the most consequential unresolved issue. Explain where a warning came from when the report shows it: what the file contains, what I noticed while loading it, whether its settings were applied, and what still needs checking. Do not imply that loading the file ran G-code on a printer. When nothing in the report needs attention, say so in a few words. Do not recite routine loading details, every notice, or file metadata. Include dimensions only when they affect the issue. Do not offer to print while the intended printer or another consequential choice is unresolved. Never claim a warning was fixed merely because its dialog was dismissed. End with your best guess at what the person wants to do next, in whatever form fits: a question, an offer or a suggested step, not a menu of alternatives.

Read each actual notice with its automatic answer and the final opening outcome. The guide below is deliberately not a code classification table.

| Notice or event you may encounter | Importance and explanation for the person |
| --- | --- |
| A newer or partly incompatible 3MF asks whether to continue | If opening succeeded, mention a lost or changed feature only when the outcome shows one. If it failed, explain the failure. Omit a version warning with no consequence. |
| Settings were substituted with supported values | Usually omit when completed successfully. Explain briefly if the result materially changes the print or still needs a choice. |
| “Customized Preset” or a file setting has no installed match | This alone does not establish that machine commands changed. Use the final selected printer and material to judge the consequence. |
| “Modified G-code” | When the notice says so, the file includes modified G-code in its printer or filament settings, and I warned about it while opening the file. G-code is the instructions a printer runs. Name the affected setting if the notice gives it and that helps locate what to review; do not invent a line number or claim I inspected the commands. Explain that these instructions need review before printing, without claiming they are safe or unsafe. Offer to review the modified G-code next. |
| Invalid values in a 3MF | If the model loaded, say which file settings need checking when their names are supplied. Do not say they were corrected unless the outcome establishes that. |
| Zero-volume parts were removed | Mention omitted parts when they could change the intended model. If nothing usable remains, lead with the failed opening. |
| “Object too small” asks whether to scale | The recorded answer says whether JusPrin scaled it. If it stayed tiny, state its final numeric size and ask the intended size. If scaled, mention the conversion only if it matters. |
| “Object too large” asks whether to shrink | The answer and final dimensions say whether it was shrunk. If still too large, explain the bed-fit problem. If shrunk, explain that its intended size may have changed. |
| A choice to open a 3MF as a project or geometry only | Use loadFacts.settingsOutcome to say whether the file's print settings were applied. Explain only when it changes the next step. |
| Connected-printer synchronization | Use the final selection and separately supplied connection state. Do not infer a connected machine from a preset name. |
| OBJ colour mapping, STEP mesh options, or unreadable STEP names | Mention a resulting colour, shape, precision or naming problem only when it matters to this model. |
| Multiple parts or files become one object | Mention grouping only if it changes how the person can print or edit the model. |
| A suggestion to simplify a very detailed model | Usually omit from the first message unless a current performance or editing problem exists. |
| A refusal to mix G-code with models, open multiple G-code files, or add models in preview mode | If the requested file did not open, explain that directly and give the next useful step. |
| “File contains no geometry” or a loading error | Lead with what failed and what, if anything, was added. Give the actual reason when available; do not invent one. |

An alarming notice does not override the final outcome. An automatic “No”, “Yes” or “OK” is JusPrin's action, not the person's preference. If several issues matter, address the most important decision first and briefly flag another consequential issue for later. If selectedSetupChange.printerPreset exists, name both its from and to selections in plain language, then ask which printer the person intends to use. Do not turn an already completed change into a fresh action item.

Use useful file author advice only when it affects the next step; keep it secondary to an unresolved printer or size decision. Attribute it to the file.

Write in uiLanguage when it is supplied. Keep it short.

---
name: live-test-built-app-on-mac
description: "How to launch, see, and drive the locally built JusPrin app on the Mac: the shared bundle id binds tools to the wrong instance, and \"on another Space\" usually means the window is on the second monitor, not that the user is in full screen."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: fa2d66ed-e217-440b-aae0-da4164953edc
  modified: 2026-09-23T18:10:30.736Z
---

Every build of the fork (and /Applications/OrcaSlicer.app) shares bundle id `com.softfever3d.orca-slicer`. The desktop-control tools resolve an app by bundle id and bind to whichever instance comes first, so `app_list_windows` returns `[]` and filtered screenshots hide the window you actually launched.

**Working recipe (2026-09-05):** `ditto` the built .app into the scratchpad, `plutil -replace CFBundleIdentifier -string com.jusprin.worktree-test`, `codesign --force --deep -s -`, then `open -n <copy>.app --args <model>` and `request_access` for the new id. `app_screenshot`/`app_click` then work and include popup menus. A display-scope `left_click` on the header did NOT open the fork's PopupWindow menus, but a background `app_click` did; take the pixel-level `zoom` with the display tools afterwards (call `app_release` first). Display-scope `Escape` does not close those popups; a click elsewhere does.

The MCP discovery file `~/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2/jusprin/mcp.json` points at the newest instance's `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp`; `tests/mcp/probe.py`'s `call()` can drive real tools (e.g. `workspace_inspect`, then `report_slice_review` with sessionId/plateId/sliceResultId) to put the header into the Check-print state without lldb. lldb `expr` cannot call inline accessors like `status_row()`.

**Why:** On 2026-09-01 a verification pass screenshotted the stock app instead of the build; on 2026-09-05 the tools bound to another session's main-repo build.

**How to apply:** Confirm the pid with `pgrep -fl OrcaSlicer.app/Contents/MacOS`; never kill an instance you did not launch. `osascript` System Events by unix id still works to set `frontmost`. See [[jusprin-shell-phase-1-design]] and [[orca-inherited-teardown-crash]].

**"On another Space" usually means "on the other monitor."** Cost about ten turns on
2026-09-09 and produced a wrong report to Kenneth. `app_list_windows` returns
`is_off_space: true` and clicks are refused with "this window is on another Space";
`app_bring_to_current_space` then fails with "the user's current Space is a full-screen
app." Both messages are about Spaces, so the natural read is that the user is sitting in
a full-screen app — but with *Displays have separate Spaces* on, a window merely sitting
on the second monitor produces exactly the same symptoms. Kenneth was not in full screen;
the harness had opened on the Acer.

Tell them apart before saying anything to the user: take a **display-scope** screenshot
(`app_release`, then `computer_batch` screenshot). Its header names the monitor it
captured and lists the others — if the window shows up there, it is a monitor problem,
not a Space problem, and the display-scope tools can drive it immediately. Never conclude
"the user is in a full-screen app" from the background tools' error text alone.

The same flag also flaps: a window can read `is_off_space: false` and click fine, then
read `true` a minute later. Clicks delivered while it is true report `ok ... unverified`
and silently do nothing. **A click that reports "unverified" and changes nothing is not
evidence of an application bug** — on 2026-09-09 that nearly became a filed defect about
being unable to retry after a failed MCP connect. Re-verify on a reachable window before
concluding anything about the app.

**Prefer the shell harness over a re-signed app copy for Agent-panel work.**
`tests/shell/.../JusPrinShellHarness.app` already carries its own bundle id
(`io.jusprin.shell-harness`), so none of the bundle-id collision above applies, and
`--manual-unconfigured` lands directly on the dock's not-set-up state — one click from
the Agent setup chooser. Build target is `shell_integration_harness`, not `shell_harness`.

**Isolate `$HOME` when testing MCP client setup.** `Mcp::default_catalog_paths()` reads
`$HOME`, so the flow will happily rewrite the real `~/.cursor/mcp.json`. Launch with
`HOME=<scratch>` holding a `.cursor/mcp.json` fixture; detection, the diff, and the write
all follow it. Force a write failure with `chmod 444` on the file **and** `555` on its
directory — the directory alone is not enough.

**Re-signed copies trigger system prompts.** Each rebuild + ad-hoc re-sign changes the cdhash, so macOS re-asks for Downloads access (recent-project thumbnail load blocks in `fopen`) and Keychain access (agent runtime reads the API key). Both are prompts only the user can answer. Avoid them by running the binary directly (`nohup <copy>.app/Contents/MacOS/OrcaSlicer --datadir <scratch copy of JusPrin2 with recent_projects cleared> <model>`) with `OPENAI_API_KEY=<placeholder>` in the environment, which short-circuits the Keychain lookup in `AgentConfiguration.cpp`. Use `sample <pid>` on the main thread to see which prompt is blocking.

**Stale as of 2026-09-18 (branch claude/printer-conversation-panel-af11cb):** `load_agent_runtime` reads the key only from app config (`jusprin_agent` / `openai_api_key`); no env var or Keychain lookup exists there. In the shell harness, `OPENAI_API_KEY` only feeds the docked pane via `install_harness_agent`; the printer panel builds its own runtime from app config, so `--printer-live` writes the key into the run's throwaway conf. Pass it as `std::string`: `AppConfig::set(section, key, const char*)` silently picks the `bool` overload and stores `true` (seen as a 401 "key rejected"). The harness temp data dir then holds the real key: delete `/var/folders/*/*/T/jusprin-shell-*` dirs from those runs afterwards.

**Hands-on printer panel with a live model (2026-09-23, jusprin-newui, uncommitted at the time):** `--manual-live-agent` now also writes `OPENAI_API_KEY` into the run's app config, so Home → "+ Add printer" gets a live printer chat. Feed the key from `~/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2/JusPrin2.conf` (`jusprin_agent.openai_api_key`) via env without echoing it. Drive it with display-scope `computer_batch` clicks/typing (background `app_click` does nothing on the web view). The scripted `--printer-live` run hangs when the model doesn't pick the printer its next "tap" step expects; kill it. Afterwards `rm -rf` the run's `/var/folders/*/*/T/jusprin-shell-*` dir — killed runs leave it behind with the key.

**Give each automated harness run a fresh scratch `$HOME`.** On 2026-09-09 a second run
against a reused scratch `$HOME` (and with a `jusprin-mcp` helper left over from the
first) never got past the Agent page handshake: it printed `HARNESS WAIT
agent_bridge_handshake preview=0 plate=0 slice_valid=1` about twice a second forever and
had to be killed at ten minutes. Runs before and after it, each with a freshly created
`$HOME` and a `pkill -f jusprin-mcp` first, finished with zero `HARNESS WAIT` lines at
all. **The cause was not isolated** — reuse and the stale helper were not separated, so
treat this as a recipe, not an explanation. `rm -rf` and recreate the scratch `$HOME`,
`pkill -f jusprin-mcp`, then run; if the handshake wait appears anyway, kill it early
rather than assuming the change under test broke the bridge.

**2026-09-19 addendum:** background `app_click` on the Home/Agent WKWebViews reports
"ok … unverified" and nothing happens; only display-scope `computer_batch` clicks
reach the page. The re-signed copy opened on the *Built-in Retina Display* while the
display tools default to the Acer, so `switch_display` first. `Return` in the composer
sends in the real app; in the built-in-browser fixture it does not (click the send
button). Another Claude session holding the computer-use lock blocks `request_access`
until Kenneth stops that session. Page-only states are cheaper via [[fake-host-page-fixture]].

content.text:
## 1. Chat panel width: done

The chat panel used to open at 320 px, which is also the narrowest you can drag it to. It now opens at 429 px, the width of the chat dock's Figma frame; the AgentUI preview tests already render the chat at that width. I added it as a new design token, `component.agentPane.width`, next to `minWidth`, the same way the left pane has both. Dragging still stops at 320, and a window too small for 429 still shrinks the panel down to 320.

- Commit `74c1335d8f` on jusprin-newui. It's local only, not pushed.
- Both token tests pass (`shell_theme_tests` and `brand_tokens_tests`).
- I launched a renamed copy of the new build with a scratch data folder and opened a cube. In a 1,403-point-wide window the chat panel was about 430 points wide. Your own running JusPrin was not touched.

## 2. The opening message after an import

I found the exact data the agent got for your screenshot in the saved conversation. Here is what it was told:

- You used **Import Object** to add arrow_headband.3mf to the "Bambu Lab A1 mini 2" setup. Its settings outcome was "geometry only", which is normal for Import Object.
- It got three notices from OrcaSlicer: the "laid over the boundary of plate" error, which arrived twice, and an object-info notice ("Size: 253.913 x 251.999 x 10 mm … <Error></Error>").
- It got the list of printers you have set up: two Kobra 3s, an A1, the A1 mini, a K1 and a Qidi X-Plus 4. It got **names only, no bed sizes**.

What makes the reply awkward, and where each problem comes from:

1. **It ends with a vague menu: "a larger printer, or split / resized".** This is the biggest problem. The bundled profiles say your A1 bed is 256 × 256 mm, the Kobra 3 is 255 × 255 and the X-Plus 4 is 305 × 305. All three fit a 254 × 252 headband. The agent couldn't say "it fits your A1" because it was never told any bed size. The file-loaded skill (its instructions for the first message after a file loads) does ask it to suggest the printer to use, but the facts it would need are missing.
2. **It narrates plumbing.** It wrote "I loaded it as geometry only, so the file's print settings were not applied", but you chose Import, so that is expected. The skill invites this with "Explain where a warning came from: … whether its settings were applied", even though a row in the skill's own table says to explain this only when it changes the next step. The two lines contradict each other.
3. **It speculates and hedges.** The skill requires a guess at what the object is, what it's for, and how to orient and support it. This part is already lying flat and 10 mm tall, and its size problem blocks everything else. So the guess turned into filler like "probably", "gently arched" and "unless you later turn it upright".
4. **It says the fit problem twice**, in the first paragraph and again in the second.
5. **"Orca reported…"** breaks the core prompt's own first-person rule.
6. **It bolds 15 phrases.** The prompt says "bold is fine" and sets no limit.

What the reply should have looked like:

> This headband is 254 × 252 mm, too big for the A1 mini's 180 × 180 mm bed. It fits your Bambu Lab A1 (256 × 256 mm). Want me to switch the project to the A1?

### Fixes I'd propose, most important first

- **A. Give the agent the fit facts.** The app would work out, for the selected printer and each printer you've set up, the bed size and whether each object fits. That goes into the file report. It follows your rule that situational text comes from the app's data, not the standing prompt. Without it, no prompt wording can produce the reply above. This is fork code, so nothing is touched in OrcaSlicer-owned files.
- **B. Cut the file-loaded skill down.** Make the object/purpose guess conditional, only when nothing blocks and it changes the setup. Remove the "explain where a warning came from" sentence. Keep one rule: name the most important problem once, then give one concrete next step.
- **C. Clean up the report.** Remove the duplicate notice. Leave out the object-info notice, since its numbers are already in `objects`.
- **D. Optionally, limit bold in the core prompt** (for example, "bold at most one phrase"). This would change every reply, not just this one, so it's a bigger decision.

Testing: I can run A–C against the recorded request with no model calls. Checking the actual wording needs live model runs, which need your OK for a specific batch. I'd suggest this file plus two or three other file-load cases, a few runs each, before and after.

Three things I need from you:
1. Should I do A, B and C together, or A first by itself?
2. Should the opening message ever guess what the object is for when nothing is blocking? Or should it just ask when the purpose matters?
3. Do you want D, or should bold stay as it is?

run it again and capture a screenshot for me to review

do you mean you run them in this session? if so, keep in mind that you are opus 5.5, a much more powerful model than the one that generated the original reponse (gpt 5 mini). you can use the current prompt to re-gen the response using yourself (opus 5.5) as the control, the tweak the prompt as you suggested

# Project chat prompt tests

The project chat's assistant is a system prompt
(`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/projectInstructions.ts`), the 28 project
tools and the chat. `run_prompt_tests.py` asks the live model for its next
step at a known point of a project chat and checks that step against one
sentence of the prompt. It is run against the prompt before an edit and after it, and the
counts compared. The app does not run.

On Kenneth's local machine, the keys are in
`~/.config/jusprin/prompt-test.env` (outside the repository, mode `600`). An
agent running this suite can load them for that command in a subshell:

```bash
( . "$HOME/.config/jusprin/prompt-test.env"; tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py )
```

Do not print, copy into the repository, or include the key values in a command
or test log. The file exports `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`; the
runner reads them from its environment. No run happens without Kenneth
approving that batch (case count, runs, token estimate). A `403 Key limit
exceeded` means stop; do not switch keys.

The model, hosts and judge are the printer suite's (`tests/printer_prompt`,
"Which model"): DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter, pinned to Alibaba,
Novita, Baidu and AtlasCloud, with a pinned OpenAI judge.

## One step, with its reads answered

Each case starts at a point recorded from the app and judges the model's next
step: a reply, or its tool calls. One response may hold several calls. The
app asks for that (`parallel_tool_calls: true`) and runs every call in the
order the model wrote it, so every call is judged here:

- A change anywhere in the response (any call the registry does not mark
  read-only) is the step, whatever came before it; the first change if
  there are several. It ends the run, and nothing is answered.
- A response of reads only is checked read by read, in order, and the first
  read the case decides on is the outcome: `issue-fix` passes on a
  `settings_get` of its setting sent after a `workspace_inspect`.
- When the case decides on none of the reads (such as `workspace_inspect`
  before a reply), every one is answered with the result the app gave for
  that read at the same point, each under its own call id, and the model is
  asked again, at most three times (`MAX_READS`, counted in responses). As
  the app does, a read after one whose result did not succeed gets the
  app's "not run" result instead.
- If any read of the response has no recorded answer, none is answered and
  the run ends unobserved, so the history never holds a call without its
  result. A fourth response of reads ends it unobserved too.

A call with arguments the registry would refuse is never answered either; it
is the step, reported beside it, and refusals are the C++ tests' business.
A run's report names every call of the response it ended on. `test_steps.py`
checks these rules offline against written model outputs, with no key and
nothing sent (`python3 tests/project_prompt/test_steps.py`).

The recorded answers, kept beside each request, are the reads the script's

# File-loaded opening message: offline experiment

Written 2026-10-19 on `jusprin-newui` at 74c1335d8f. Untracked working doc.

## What was tested

The case is Kenneth's import of `arrow_headband.3mf` onto "Bambu Lab A1 mini 2". The object is 253.9 × 252.0 × 10 mm and the bed is 180 × 180 mm. The app's first message, from gpt-5.4-mini (the default in `OpenAIResponsesAgent.hpp`), was awkward: it narrated how the file was loaded, guessed at the object and its slicing, stated the fit problem twice, ended with a menu of options and bolded 11 phrases.

I rebuilt the request from the code and from the saved conversation (`~/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2/jusprin/projects/p-3a6318012e2f827f-2d66758b462735b3/current-state.json`):

- the system prompt from `projectInstructions.ts`;
- the 28 tools from `tests/project_prompt/project_tools.json`;
- the file report exactly as saved;
- a `<workspace>` block written by hand from the saved checkpoint;
- the file-loaded skill text plus the "nothing is recorded about what this print is for" sentence.

Each run was a fresh Opus 5.5 subagent that saw only that request, never this critique. Three limits apply:

- The picture is a crop of Kenneth's screenshot, not the app's own render.
- Tool calls could not be answered, so a run that wanted a call named it and replied from what it had.
- Opus 5.5 is a far stronger model than gpt-5.4-mini. Only a live batch on gpt-5.4-mini shows whether these changes carry over to it.

## Variants

- **v0 (control):** the request as the app sent it.
- **v1a (data only):** the same skill, but the report is changed in two ways. Each `setupPrinters` entry gains `bedMm`, the usable bed after the profile's excluded areas. The object gains `fitsSelectedPrinter: false` and `fitsOn: ["Bambu Lab A1", "Qidi X-Plus 4"]`. The duplicate boundary notice and the object-info notice (whose numbers are already in `objects`) are removed.
- **v1b (data + skill):** v1a's report plus the rewritten skill (diff at the end).

The Kobra 3 is a trap for raw bed sizes. Its profile says 255 × 255 mm but excludes a 2 mm border, so only 251 mm is usable and the 254 mm headband does not fit. A field holding the nominal bed size would have told the model it fits. The app has to report the result of the fit check, not just the size.

## Results (3 runs each)

| | words | bold phrases | names A1 as the fix | object guess | PLA/PETG tangent | "when I opened the file I warned" | ends with one question |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| gpt-5.4-mini, original | 132 | 11 | no ("a larger printer") | yes | no | "Orca reported" | no (a menu) |
| v0 Opus | 190–230 | 3–5 | 3/3 (2 of 3 wrongly call the Kobra 3 too small... which happens to be right, for the wrong reason) | 3/3 | 3/3 | 2/3 | 3/3 |
| v1a Opus | 200–260 | 3–6 | 3/3 | 3/3 | 3/3 | 3/3 | 2/3 |
| v1b Opus | 60–110 | 2–4 | 3/3 | 1/3, one sentence | 0/3 | 0/3 | 3/3 |

Conclusions:

- The data change makes the printer advice correct: bed sizes, the Kobra 3's exclusion, the 1 mm margin on the A1.
- The skill rewrite is what fixes the length and the awkward parts. The current skill tells the model to guess the object and its slicing, and to explain where a warning came from, so even Opus does both.
- Bold was not changed. Opus bolds 2–6 phrases under the same prompt, and the saved gpt replies on this machine bold heavily on Sep 30 and since Oct 12 (both before and after "bold are fine" was added on Oct 15) but not at all from Oct 1 to 10. The saved conversations don't record which model or prompt produced each reply, so the cause can't be pinned without live runs.

## Representative replies

### gpt-5.4-mini, original (what Kenneth saw)

> The big issue is fit: the model is **253.9 × 252.0 × 10 mm**, and Orca reported it **extends past the plate boundary**. I loaded it as **geometry only**, so the file's print settings were **not** applied.
>
> From the picture and the name, I'd guess this is a **headband / arched wearable part**. It probably wants to be printed **flat or gently arched**, with the **largest flat face on the bed** and **no supports** unless you later turn it upright. Right now it also looks much too wide for the **A1 mini** plate setup, so the selected printer/preset combo may be the wrong choice for this model.
>
> I'd start by checking whether you meant to print it on a **larger printer** or whether it needs to be **split / resized** before slicing.

### v0, Opus, run 2

> **This won't fit on the printer that's selected now.** The headband is about 254 × 252 mm across. The selected printer, the Bambu Lab A1 mini, has a bed of only 180 × 180 mm. That's why I showed the "laid over the boundary of plate" error when the file opened. Nothing has fixed it yet, and turning the model on the bed won't help, because the arrow already runs corner to corner.
>
> Two of the printers you've set up are big enough:
> - **Bambu Lab A1** (256 × 256 mm bed): it fits, but with only about a millimetre to spare on each side. There's no room for a brim, the extra ring of plastic some prints use to grip the bed.
> - **Qidi X-Plus 4** (305 × 305 mm bed): it fits with room to spare.
>
> The Kobra 3 and K1 beds are too small for it.
>
> My guess is that this is a costume headband with the "arrow through the head" gag. It's only 10 mm tall, so it can print flat, just as it lies now, and shouldn't need supports, which are temporary props printed under overhanging parts. The band has to flex to go on your head, and plain PLA can snap when it's bent like that. A more flexible material such as PETG would hold up better. If you stay with PLA, the Textured Cool Plate you have selected now is a good match for it.
>
> Which printer do you plan to print this on? Is it the A1, or the Qidi?

### v1a, Opus, run 2

> **This model doesn't fit on the printer that's selected now.** It's about 254 × 252 mm, and the Bambu Lab A1 mini's bed is only 180 × 180 mm. That's why I warned, while opening the file, that the object sticks out past the edge of the plate. I didn't shrink or move it. It's still full size and still hangs over the edges.
>
> Two of the printers you've set up can hold it at this size:
> - **Bambu Lab A1** (256 × 256 mm). It's a tight fit, with only about a millimetre to spare on each side.
> - **Qidi X-Plus 4** (305 × 305 mm). This one leaves plenty of room.
>
> The other way to make it fit the A1 mini is to scale it down by about 30%, but then it probably won't fit around a head.
>
> My guess is that this is a costume headband with an "arrow through the head" look. The two arrow ends would sit on either side of your head. It's lying flat and is only 10 mm tall, so it can print just as it sits, with no supports. The thin band has to bend to slip on, and PLA (your current material) can snap when it's bent like that. PETG bends more before it breaks, if you have some.
>
> Which printer do you want to print it on? If it's the A1, I'll switch to it and its matching 0.20mm Standard settings.

### v1b, Opus, all three runs

Run 1:

> This arrow headband is about **254 × 252 mm** across, too big for the selected **Bambu Lab A1 mini 2**. That printer's bed is 180 × 180 mm, so right now the arrow and band hang off the plate.
>
> Two of the printers you've set up can hold it:
> - **Bambu Lab A1** (256 × 256 mm bed). It fits, with only about 1 mm to spare on each side.
> - **Qidi X-Plus 4** (305 × 305 mm bed). It fits with plenty of room.
>
> The Anycubic Kobra 3 bed is just too small, at 251 mm.
>
> Which printer do you want to print it on? I'll switch the setup to that one.

Run 2:

> This **arrow headband** is about 254 × 252 mm across. That's too big for the bed of your selected **Bambu Lab A1 mini 2**, which is 180 × 180 mm, so right now it hangs off the plate and won't slice. It's only 10 mm tall, so it fits two of your other printers: your **Bambu Lab A1** (256 × 256 mm, with only a couple of millimetres to spare) and your **Qidi X-Plus 4** (305 × 305 mm). The material (Generic PLA) and the print settings (0.20mm Standard) are fine for now. We can fine-tune them once the printer is settled.
>
> Do you want me to switch the setup to your Bambu Lab A1?

Run 3:

> **This model is too big for the selected printer.** The arrow headband is about 254 × 252 mm, and the Bambu Lab A1 mini's bed is only 180 × 180 mm, so it hangs off the plate in the picture. Of the printers you've set up, it fits on your **Bambu Lab A1** (256 × 256 mm bed) and the **Qidi X-Plus 4**. The A1 is the closer match, since it uses the same kind of Bambu setup you have selected now.
>
> It looks like a novelty "arrow through the head" headband. It's only 10 mm tall, so it should print flat on the plate as it is.
>
> Shall I switch the printer to the Bambu Lab A1?

## Skill change tested in v1b

The first paragraph's setupPrinters sentence gains:

> …each with bedMm, the usable bed (width, depth, height) after any area its profile excludes. An object's fitsSelectedPrinter and fitsOn are the app's own check of its size, as placed, against those beds.

The two paragraphs "Look at the attached picture… make an educated guess at what the object is, what it is likely for, and how it should be sliced…" and "Write one useful message… Explain where a warning came from…" are replaced by:

> Look at the attached picture when there is one. Check the selected printer, filament and process presets and the plate type against the file and against the printers the person has set up; when one looks wrong for this print, say which and suggest the one to use, without changing it. When an object does not fit the selected printer, name the set-up printer it fits, from fitsOn.
>
> Write a short message, a few sentences, about what matters for this file now:
> - Lead with what decides whether or how it can print: a load that failed, an object that does not fit, a printer to choose, settings or G-code that need review. Say it once, with only the numbers that matter.
> - Say what you take the object to be, and how it should be printed, only when that changes the advice, and then briefly, as a guess. Leave other advice (material, strength, orientation) until the main decision is made.
> - Do not explain routine loading: how the file was opened, whether its settings were applied, or which notices appeared, unless it changes the next step. Do not imply that loading the file ran G-code on a printer. Never claim a warning was fixed merely because its dialog was dismissed.
> - When nothing needs attention, say so in a sentence.
> - End with one question or offer about the next step, not a menu of alternatives. Do not offer to print while the intended printer or another consequential choice is unresolved.

The notice table and the paragraphs after it are unchanged. The experiment files (request assembler, variants, the cropped picture) are in this session's scratchpad under `exp/`.

I sent the chat-panel screenshot. I also re-ran the headband request offline with Opus 5.5, as you suggested. Rewriting the skill fixes it, and adding bed facts to the file report makes the printer advice correct. Nothing in the repo has changed for this yet. All nine replies, the table and the exact skill wording are in [file-loaded-opening-experiment.md](file-loaded-opening-experiment.md), which is untracked.

**Screenshot.** The test copy has no agent key, so the panel shows "No agent connected". It opened the 3MF as a project, so the printer shown is the file's P1S. The panel is 429 points wide in a 1,403-point window.

**How I ran it.** You were right about the model. The app's default is gpt-5.4-mini (in `OpenAIResponsesAgent.hpp`), not gpt-5-mini, but still much weaker than me. I rebuilt the exact request the app sent: the system prompt, the 28 tools, the saved file report, the workspace block and the skill text. I gave it to fresh Opus 5.5 subagents that never saw my critique, three runs per variant. Three limits:

Write `cd "$S"; nohup harness ... &`. Check with `pgrep -fl "<worktree>.*JusPrinShellHarness"` before finishing.

"""render.py <case dir> <variant> : writes <case>/<variant>/request.md and picture.png
Variant transforms live in variants.py: transform(body, case) -> body."""
import json,sys,base64,pathlib,importlib.util,glob
case=pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]); variant=sys.argv[2]
spec=importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('variants', pathlib.Path(__file__).parent/'variants.py'); V=importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(V)
body=json.load(open(sorted(glob.glob(str(case/'*-turn.json')))[0]))
body=V.VARIANTS[variant](body, case.name)
out=case/variant; out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
lines=["# API request (OpenAI Responses API shape)","","## instructions",body['instructions'],"","## tools",json.dumps(body['tools'],indent=1,ensure_ascii=False),"","## input, in order"]
for i,it in enumerate(body['input'],1):
    lines.append(f"\n### item {i} — role: {it.get('role')}")
    c=it['content']
    if isinstance(c,str): lines.append(c); continue
    for j,p in enumerate(c,1):
        if p['type']=='input_image':
            png=base64.b64decode(p['image_url'].split(',',1)[1]); (out/'picture.png').write_bytes(png)
            lines.append(f"part {j} (input_image: the file {out/'picture.png'} — open it with the Read tool)")
        else: lines.append(f"part {j} (text):\n{p['text']}")
(out/'request.md').write_text('\n'.join(lines)); print(out/'request.md')
EOF
echo ok

input.content:
# File-loaded opening message: offline experiments

Untracked working doc, 2026-10-19, `jusprin-newui` at 74c1335d8f. All replies from round 2 are in `file-loaded-opening-replies.md` next to this file. Nothing in the repository has been changed for this.

## The question

When a person opens or imports a file, the app sends the agent a file-load report, a `<workspace>` block, a picture of the plate and the file-loaded skill (the instructions for that one message). The agent then writes its first message. On Kenneth's headband import that message was awkward and missed the obvious fix. Round 1 found one missing fact (bed sizes). Kenneth's objection was that adding one field per problem we happen to hit is patchwork. Round 2 therefore chooses the report's facts from everything the app can know, and tests on several different files instead of one.

## Method

- **Real requests.** I pointed a test copy of the app (its own data folder, Kenneth's printers and presets, A1 mini selected) at a local server that saves each request and answers with an error (`JUSPRIN_OPENAI_ENDPOINT`). Opening a file then records the exact request the app would send to gpt-5.4-mini: system prompt, 28 tools, report, workspace block, the app's own render and the skill. Nothing was sent to OpenAI.
- **Extra facts from the app itself.** For each file I also called the app's own MCP tools (`object_analyze` with mesh, fit and orientations; `workspace_inspect`). I read the printers' beds from their profiles and the 3MF's own settings from inside the file.
- **Stand-in model.** Each request went to a fresh Opus 5.5 subagent that saw only that request and picture. It gets one run per case and variant. Tool calls could not be answered.
- **Variants.**
  - **v0:** the request unchanged.
  - **v1:** the rewritten skill.
  - **v2:** the rewritten skill plus the chosen facts.

Limits: Opus 5.5 is much stronger than gpt-5.4-mini, there is one run per cell, and I judged the replies myself. A live gpt-5.4-mini batch is what would settle it. That needs Kenneth's approval.

## Cases

| Case | File | Situation |
|---|---|---|
| battery | Battery_Holder_AAAandAA.stl | Plain part, nothing wrong |
| octopus | Octopus_v6.stl | Print-in-place figure, nothing wrong |
| tiny | Swanky Wolt-Blad.stl | 22 mm L-piece standing on thin edges |
| yoda | YodaFigure.stl | 150 mm figure, 1.26M triangles, simplify notice |
| frame_parts | All frame parts.3mf | PrusaSlicer 3MF; JusPrin loads geometry only; 32 parts |
| headband | arrow_headband.3mf (imported) | Too big for the A1 mini (Kenneth's case) |
| two_color | little_boxes_two_color.3mf | Opening it switched to the file's "MyKlipper 0.6 nozzle" and PA-CF; the object is partly off the plate |
| bambu_project | FFZW迫击炮P1X1系列无裙边.3mf | Bambu P1S project, 13 parts, collision warning, Chinese text |

## How the facts were chosen

A read-only survey listed everything the report and workspace carry today, what the tools can return, and what OrcaSlicer knows after a load that neither exposes, with the cost of each. I then kept a fact only if it answers one of the questions a first message has to settle, and only if it is cheap enough to compute at load time.

| Question the first message must settle | Fact | Today | Cost | Round 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Did the file open, and did it change my setup? | loadFacts | sent | — | unchanged |
| Can it print on the selected printer? | `placedOnBed` (OrcaSlicer's instance print-volume state) and `fitsSelectedBed` (size vs usable bed) | no; only OrcaSlicer's notice text, which means either | in memory / cheap | added |
| If not, which of my printers can? | `bedMm` per set-up printer (usable, after excluded areas); `fitsSetupPrinters` | names only | cheap | added |
| Is the model sound? | `mesh`: triangles, shells, open edges, repaired errors | only through `object_analyze` | computed at load | added |
| Is the scale right? | `unitsSuspicion` (inches or metres) | only through `object_analyze` | cheap | added when not "none" (no case exercised it) |
| How should it sit on the bed? | `asPlaced` overhang and bed contact; `betterOrientation` when much better | only through `object_analyze` | mesh pass; several minutes on the 1.26M-triangle Yoda | added, to measure its value |
| What did the file expect? | `file`: app that saved it, printer and nozzle it was made for, filament slots, painted colours | lost on a geometry-only load; otherwise only as preset names | cheap, but must be captured inside OrcaSlicer's `load_files` | added |
| Was it already prepared? | painted supports or seams, modifiers, layer ranges | partly | in memory | not exercised by these files |
| (noise) | duplicate notices; OrcaSlicer's object-info notice; `overrideCount` | sent | — | duplicates and object-info removed; `overrideCount` left in |

Left out on purpose:
- faces and holes (a heavy mesh pass);
- anything that needs a slice (support volume, time, weight);
- marketplace IDs and other metadata;
- connected-printer detail beyond its model (no case exercised it).

## Results

| Case | v0 (today) | v1 (skill) | v2 (skill + facts) |
|---|---|---|---|
| battery | 198 words: guessed purpose, orientation/support/material bullets, "check your plate" | 78 words, ready, one question | 116 words, ready ("no errors, very little prints over empty space") |
| octopus | 209 words of guesses and bullets | 101 words | 110 words |
| tiny | 202 words; calls standing on edge "the best way" | 113 words; first-layer caution | 107 words: **"lay one wall flat, contact 64 → 660 mm², no overhang"**, which only the orientation fact made possible |
| yoda | 246 words, layer and support advice | 107 words, supports | 138 words, supports, "no holes or errors" |
| frame_parts | 290 words, suggests finer presets | 138 words | 132 words |
| headband | 232 words; right printers from the model's own knowledge, Kobra 3 bed wrong | 115 words; picks the Qidi, gives the Kobra 3 as 250 mm (it is 251 usable) | 131 words; A1 or Qidi from `fitsSetupPrinters`; "switch rather than resize" |
| two_color | 363 words; **"too wide", wrong** | 181 words; **"doesn't fit the plate", wrong** | 142 words; **"hangs over the edge, has to be moved, doesn't need resizing"**, correct |
| bambu_project | 274 words | 135 words | 143 words; "every piece fits each of your printers" |

What this shows:

1. **The skill rewrite fixes the tone and length on every kind of file, not only the headband.** Median length goes from about 240 words to about 115. Today's skill requires an object guess, an orientation/supports/strength discussion and a warning-origin explanation, so even Opus writes all three for a battery holder that needs nothing.
2. **The facts fix correctness, and two of the three corrections were cases I had not looked for.**
   - **two_color:** OrcaSlicer's "laid over the boundary of plate" text covers both "too big" and "placed off the edge". Without `placedOnBed` and `fitsSelectedBed`, both v0 and v1 told the person a 244 × 129 mm object was too big for a 250 × 250 mm bed. With them, v2 said to move it.
   - **tiny:** the orientation fact turned a vague first-layer caution into a concrete fix.
   - **headband:** the bed sizes replaced guessed numbers.
3. **No fact made the replies worse.** The mesh facts mostly produce a short "no holes or errors" clause. The model ignored 193 shells on Yoda and 57 on the octopus, which is right.
4. **`overrideCount: 1` is noise.** Every freshly loaded STL carries it. Four runs stopped to wonder what it is, though none put it in the reply. Its cause is unverified.

Bold: Opus used 0–9 bold phrases per reply under every variant. That's no evidence either way about gpt-5.4-mini's heavy bolding, so nothing was changed for it.

## App defects found along the way (not fixed)

- **Blank picture.** The two_color render the app attached is completely empty: the object is partly off the plate, and the render shows nothing at all. The agent gets no picture exactly when it needs one.
- **Turn with no report.** Opening `Cura_Plus4-Pla.3mf` loaded no objects and saved no report, yet the app still started an agent turn whose only input was the workspace block. That case was dropped from the set.
- **Slow orientation scoring.** `object_analyze` with orientations on Yoda kept the app busy for several minutes. So `asPlaced` and `betterOrientation` can't be computed on every load as is. They need a cheaper current-orientation-only measure, a triangle cap, or to run after the first message.

## Proposed next steps (not started)

1. Add the facts in the table to the report: fit split into placed vs fits, beds of set-up printers, mesh health, units, file facts captured inside `load_files`, prepared-ness flags. Remove the duplicate and object-info notices, and decide what `overrideCount` should mean.
2. Decide orientation separately, once its cost on large meshes is measured properly.
3. Keep iterating the skill with this harness. The case set and recorder can be re-run in about 10 minutes, so every skill edit can be measured across all eight files.
4. Then one live gpt-5.4-mini batch on the same eight recorded requests, v0 vs the final variant (needs Kenneth's approval).

## Round 1 (headband only), for the record

This round used three runs each on a hand-rebuilt headband request:
- today's request;
- data only (bed sizes and a fit list);
- data plus the rewritten skill.

Data alone made the printer advice right but left the reply long. Only the skill rewrite fixed the tone. Round 2 confirms both findings across the eight files.

## Skill text tested (v2)

The rewrite replaced the paragraphs "Look at the attached picture… make an educated guess at what the object is, what it is likely for, and how it should be sliced…" and "Write one useful message… Explain where a warning came from…" with:

> Look at the attached picture when there is one. Check the selected printer, filament and process presets and the plate type against the file and against the printers the person has set up; when one looks wrong for this print, say which and suggest the one to use, without changing it. When an object does not fit the selected printer, name a set-up printer it fits, from fitsSetupPrinters.
>
> Write a short message, a few sentences, about what matters for this file now:
> - Lead with what decides whether or how it can print: a load that failed, an object that does not fit, a printer to choose, settings or G-code that need review. Say it once, with only the numbers that matter.
> - Say what you take the object to be, and how it should be printed, only when that changes the advice, and then briefly, as a guess. Leave other advice (material, strength, orientation) until the main decision is made.
> - Do not explain routine loading: how the file was opened, whether its settings were applied, or which notices appeared, unless it changes the next step. Do not imply that loading the file ran G-code on a printer. Never claim a warning was fixed merely because its dialog was dismissed.
> - When nothing needs attention, say so in a sentence.
> - End with one question or offer about the next step, not a menu of alternatives. Do not offer to print while the intended printer or another consequential choice is unresolved.

v2 also adds, after the setupPrinters sentence, a description of each new field. The core of it: "an object that is off the bed but fits it needs moving, not resizing". The notice table is unchanged.

The experiment files (recorder, case recorder, probe, renderer, variants, every request and reply) are in this session's scratchpad under `exp/`.

content.text:
I agree, and that's how I redid it. I started from what the app knows when a file loads, kept the facts that help the first message decide something, and tested on eight different files instead of the headband alone. The rewritten skill fixed the tone and length on every file. The chosen facts corrected two replies that were wrong or vague, and neither of those was a problem I had gone looking for. The skill is not finalized and nothing in the repo has changed. The write-up is [file-loaded-opening-experiment.md](file-loaded-opening-experiment.md), with every reply in [file-loaded-opening-replies.md](file-loaded-opening-replies.md); both are untracked.

**How the facts were chosen.** A read-only survey listed what the report sends today, what the agent's tools can return, and what OrcaSlicer knows after a load but never passes on, with the cost of each. I kept a fact only if it answers a question the first message has to settle:
- Did the file change my setup?
- Can it print on the selected printer, and if not, on which of my printers?
- Is the model sound, and is it the right scale?
- How should it sit on the bed?
- What did the file expect: which printer, which filaments, any painted colours?

Facts that need a slice or a heavy mesh pass stayed behind tools.

**How it was tested.** Each file was opened in a test copy of the app whose agent pointed at a local recorder. That gave the exact request gpt-5.4-mini would get, including the app's own picture, and nothing went to OpenAI. The extra facts came from the app's own tools, the printer profiles and the 3MF files. Each request went to a fresh Opus 5.5 subagent, one run per file and version, in three versions: today's request (v0), the rewritten skill (v1), and the rewritten skill plus the facts (v2).

**Results:**
- **Today's skill makes even Opus long-winded.** v0 replies run 198–363 words. A battery holder that needs nothing still gets a guess at what it is, bullets on orientation, supports and material, and "check your plate".
- **The skill rewrite fixes tone and length everywhere.** v1 replies run 78–181 words and lead with what matters.
- **The facts fixed things I hadn't anticipated:**
  - **Two-colour boxes:** OrcaSlicer's "laid over the boundary of plate" message means either "too big" or "placed off the edge". v0 and v1 both told the person a 244 × 129 mm object was too big for a 250 × 250 mm bed. With the facts "not placed on the bed" and "fits the bed", v2 correctly said to move it.
  - **22 mm corner piece:** it stands on thin edges with 64 mm² touching the bed. With the orientation fact, v2 suggested laying a wall flat, which gives 660 mm² of contact and no overhang. Without it, the replies only said to watch the first layer.
  - **Headband:** real bed sizes replaced the model's guesses. Without them, v1 gave the Kobra 3 as 250 mm; its usable width is 251.
- **No fact made a reply worse.** The mesh-health facts mostly add a short "no holes or errors".
- **One field is noise.** `overrideCount: 1` appears on every freshly loaded STL, and four runs stopped to wonder what it meant. Its cause is unverified.

**Limits:** one run per cell, Opus instead of gpt-5.4-mini, and I judged the replies myself.

**App defects found along the way (not fixed):**
- **Blank picture:** the picture the app attaches is completely empty when the object is partly off the plate, which is exactly when it is needed.
- **Turn with no report:** opening a Cura 3MF loaded nothing and saved no report, yet the app still started an agent turn with only the workspace block.
- **Slow orientation check:** the orientation check kept the app busy for several minutes on the 1.26-million-triangle Yoda model. It can't run on every load as it is now.

**Decisions for you:**
1. Should I build the chosen facts into the report? That means placed vs fits, the bed of each printer you've set up, mesh health, units, and the file's own facts captured during the load, plus removing the noisy notices. Orientation would wait until its cost is solved.
2. Should I keep refining the skill with this test setup? It re-runs all eight files in a few minutes. It lives in my temporary scratch folder, so I'd move it into the repo if you want to keep it.
3. Once the skill settles, may I run one live gpt-5.4-mini batch on these eight recorded requests, today's version against the final one?
1. yes. 2. no more refining. 3. no more runs

Got it. I'll build the chosen facts into the file-load report, with no more skill iterations and no more model runs. One reading I'm taking from "no more refining": the v2 skill text is final as tested. It goes in as a separate commit after the facts commit, so you can drop it if you didn't mean that.

184 agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md
# Fork stewardship

**Status:** Required discipline for every change to an upstream-owned file on `jusprin-newui`.

JusPrin is a long-lived fork. Every line it changes in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line it re-resolves at every rebase, forever, by a person who was not there when the line was written. The rules below exist to keep that permanent cost small and, where it cannot be small, to keep it visible.

One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**

- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.

Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.

## The ten principles

### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much

**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.

**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.

**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?

**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.

### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge

**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.

**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.

**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?

**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.

### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it

**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.

**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.

**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?

**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.

### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism

**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.

**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.

**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?

**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.

### 5. One seam beats many touch points

**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.

**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.

**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?

**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.

### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict

**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.

**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.

**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.

**Violation.** Writing a second object-duplication routine next to OrcaSlicer's clipboard path and pointing an existing dialog at it. Reusing the existing path — extending it where it was too narrow — keeps one implementation.

### 7. Unavoidable conflicts must be easy to resolve correctly

**Rule.** When you must delete or relocate an upstream line, say at the site what moved, where it went, and what a future rebase must carry across.

**Mechanism.** The real cost of a conflict is not the stop; it is the chance of resolving it wrongly. Appending near an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — keep both — is right. Deleting an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — take mine, the logic moved — silently discards whatever upstream did to that line in the meantime.

**The test.** Six months from now, is the natural resolution of the conflict I am creating the correct one? If not, what does the resolver need to read to get it right, and is that text next to the conflict?

**Violation.** Removing an upstream snapshot label that upstream later localized. Git stops for a human, but the intent-faithful resolution throws the translation away, and nothing at the site says otherwise.

### 8. Do not diverge where you gain nothing; converge where upstream already went

**Rule.** No gratuitous formatting, reordering, or whitespace differences. Before reverting a cosmetic difference, compare against current upstream — it may have made the same change.

**Mechanism.** Every valueless difference is a conflict site that buys nothing. And if upstream has independently arrived at your version, "fixing" it back creates divergence rather than removing it. Adopting a change upstream has already made converges the two trees early and makes the eventual conflict resolve itself.

**The test.** Does this difference carry meaning? Has upstream already made it?

**Violation.** Consuming a shared blank line in a list of build subdirectories, where upstream also appends entries.

### 9. Verify the risk claim instead of reasoning about it

**Rule.** Before asserting that a change is or is not rebase-risky, check it. Three checks, each one command: does git actually conflict there; has upstream already converged on the same change; is the change a move or a duplication.

**Mechanism.** A coherent story about fork risk is not a true one, and every one of these is cheaper to check than to argue about. Reasoning alone reliably produces confident, wrong claims — that a lost change is "silent" when git stops for it, that a move is a "duplication," that a cosmetic difference is gratuitous when upstream shares it.

**The test.** Did I run the simulation, or am I describing what I expect it to say?

**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.

### 10. Pull direction dominates every local edit

**Rule.** Replay the fork's own commits onto upstream. Never merge upstream in, and never rebase the whole branch.

**Mechanism.** The fork's own footprint is small; the inherited release-branch history is not. Merging upstream in makes the conflict surface the entire divergence between the release branch and upstream's development line — none of it ours. Rebasing only our commits discards that inherited history by taking upstream's version of every file we never touched.

**The test.** Am I replaying our commits onto upstream, or bringing upstream into ours?

**Violation.** `git merge upstream/main`, which produces a conflict list dominated by vendor profiles, translations, and CI files that JusPrin has never edited.

## Before you finish

A change that touches upstream-owned files is not done until this is recorded in the handback or pull request:

1. **The rebase simulation and its result.** Run it against current upstream and name both endpoint commits — measurements are not reproducible otherwise.

   ```bash
   git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<fork base> upstream/main HEAD
   ```

   For each conflicted file, state whether the natural resolution is correct or lossy. A lossy one is a defect to fix now, not a note for later.

2. **An account of every upstream line deleted or rewritten.** Where the logic went, and why an additive form was not possible.

3. **A statement of what the fork now owns.** Policy, a neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.

An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.

## This fork's terrain

Facts specific to OrcaSlicer, worth knowing before choosing where to put a seam. They change over time; re-measure rather than trusting these.

`Plater.cpp` is by far the busiest file the fork touches, followed by the central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt`, `GLCanvas3D.cpp`, and `PartPlate.cpp`. `GLToolbar` and `GLGizmosManager` are quiet. File-level churn is only a first approximation: some functions inside `Plater.cpp` have not been touched upstream in the entire life of this fork, and a seam there is far cheaper than the file's overall rate suggests. Measure the function, not just the file.

Some native state is shared rather than owned by one object. OrcaSlicer's collapse toolbar belongs to `Plater` and is used by both the Prepare and Preview canvases, so a per-canvas guard cannot save and restore it correctly. Shared state needs one owner at the shared lifetime boundary, and exact restoration needs a getter as well as a setter.

`MainFrame`'s Notebook is cheaper to wrap than to dismantle. Dozens of
upstream predicates — menu and shortcut enabling, `can_delete`, slice status
updates, undo/redo gating — key off `m_tabpanel->GetSelection()`, so removing
or reparenting the Prepare/Preview pages breaks them with no conflict and no
error. A shell gets a tabless full-window layout for free instead: hide the
strip via the public `GetBtnsListCtrl()` (wxBookCtrlBase gives a hidden
controller zero size, so pages fill the client area), and the stock slice and
print side buttons disappear with it because `ButtonsListCtrl` reparents them
into the strip at construction. The Phase 1 production shell reached a
19-added-line upstream footprint this way where the POC's reparenting shell
needed edits across eight upstream files.

The same measurement gives the rule for every fork-owned screen that comes
after the shell. OrcaSlicer's surfaces (the stock homepage, Prepare, Preview,
Monitor, the settings tabs) stay inside the Notebook, because their
correctness depends on it. Fork-owned surfaces (the header, the Agent pane,
Home, and whatever follows) live outside it, as siblings of the Notebook in a
fork-owned sizer, shown and hidden by the shell. The shell *reads* the
Notebook's selection to decide what to show and *never edits its page list*:
no `RemovePage`, `InsertPage`, or reparenting of a stock page. Removing or
replacing a page hands the fork the meaning of that index. Upstream keeps
addressing it by number — `tpHome` as a dialog parent, the target of
`EVT_LOAD_URL`, the tab `post_init` returns to — and every one of those lands
on the fork's widget with no conflict and no error. If a fork surface truly
must be a page, append it last, where no upstream code addresses it.

Navigation between screens stays a Notebook selection change even when the
screen being left is fork-owned. Menu and shortcut enabling, undo and redo
availability, and slice-status updates all read `GetSelection()`, so the
selection must remain the one record of which OrcaSlicer surface is active.
Showing Prepare any other way leaves those predicates answering for the wrong
page, silently.

Some stock behavior is already exposed as an event idiom rather than a
function. Upstream itself drives plate slicing from two places with the same
sequence — the slice button and the Cmd+R shortcut both run
`plater->update(true, true)`, post `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_PLATE` to the Plater,
and select the Preview tab — so fork code may repeat that short dispatch
without violating the shared-implementation rule; the behavior itself stays
owned by Plater's event handler.

Historical measurements and the incidents behind several of these rules are in the [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) and, for the spike era, in the [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

input.prompt:
Add a backend to tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py (and, if it shares the code, tests/printer_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py) that answers each recorded step with the locally installed Claude Code CLI in headless mode, instead of POSTing to OpenRouter (model) and OpenAI (judge). The goal is prompt iteration that bills the developer's Claude subscription, not API usage.

What exists: the runner replays requests recorded from the app (tests/project_prompt/requests.json, recorded by the shell harness). It sends each one to deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash on OpenRouter (MODEL, ENDPOINT, post()). It answers read-only tool calls from recorded results, at most three reads (recorded_answer, answers_for, run_once, MAX_READS). It judges the step with JUDGE_MODEL gpt-5.5 over the OpenAI API (judge(), judge_response()). The README in tests/project_prompt explains the step rules. test_steps.py checks them offline.

Design to implement, keeping all of today's step rules:
- New flag, e.g. `--backend claude-cli [--claude-model opus]`. The default stays as today.
- Per run: `claude -p --model <m> --system-prompt <the request's instructions> --tools "" --strict-mcp-config --mcp-config <generated json> --output-format stream-json --no-session-persistence`. The 2.1.283 CLI has all of these flags; verify the exact behaviour, and whether `--bare` keeps subscription auth.
- Real tool calling through a small stdio MCP stub server written in Python under tests/project_prompt/. It exposes the 28 tools from project_tools.json with their real schemas. Read-only calls are answered with today's recorded answers. The first change call is recorded as the step and ends the run, exactly as today. Parse which tool calls happened from the stream-json output.

- Judge on the subscription too (`claude -p --json-schema` for a yes/no verdict), behind its own flag, because changing the judge resets the baselines (see the "confirmed results become the baseline" convention in the README/handoffs).
- Run several cases in parallel with a small cap, so the subscription's rate limits aren't hit all at once.
- README: when to use which backend. Opus on the subscription measures what the prompt itself causes, and is cheap to iterate with. The app's default model is gpt-5.4-mini (OpenAIResponsesAgent.hpp), which scored about like DeepSeek in the README's model table. So a strong model can paper over ambiguities a weaker one trips on, and a small paid run on the app's default stays the pre-release check.

content.text:
**Commit:** there was nothing to commit. No code had changed for the report facts yet, and the two write-ups are untracked working docs that stay uncommitted. I moved the implementation, with every design decision so far, to its own session: [Add chosen facts to the file-load report](#local_4514e803-fed9-427a-96d5-ea65e92ed8bc).

**Prompt testing:** you're mostly right. One correction: recording isn't new. Today's prompt tests already replay requests recorded from the app, in `tests/project_prompt/requests.json`. What differs is who answers them:

- **Today:** each run sends the recorded request to DeepSeek V4 Flash on OpenRouter, then has gpt-5.5 judge the step over the OpenAI API. Both are billed per token.
- **This session:** I captured requests by pointing the app at a local recorder, and fresh Opus 5.5 subagents read each request and wrote the reply. That ran on the subscription.

I agree the subscription is the better default for iterating on prompts. Two things to keep in mind:

1. **The app's default model isn't stronger than DeepSeek.** It's gpt-5.4-mini, and it scored about the same as DeepSeek in the printer tests' model comparison (82 vs 79 of 87). A strong model can paper over prompt ambiguities a weaker one trips on; Opus filled in bed sizes from its own knowledge, for example. Opus is good at showing what the prompt itself causes. That's what found the forced object guesses this session. I'd still keep a small paid run on the app's default model as a check before release.
2. **The subagent method I used is too loose for a test suite.** The subagents read a Markdown dump, couldn't make real tool calls, knew they were being tested (several added notes about it), and I judged the replies myself.

The installed CLI (Claude Code 2.1.283) supports a tighter version. The existing Python runner could call headless `claude -p` with:

- the app's own instructions as the system prompt (`--system-prompt`),
- built-in tools turned off (`--tools ""`),
- a small MCP stub server exposing the 28 real tools, answering reads from the recordings.

That gives real tool calls, the same step rules as today, and a judge on the subscription too. I haven't checked whether `--bare` keeps subscription sign-in, or whether images pass through in the headless input format.

The card below proposes building that. It starts with one case end to end so you can see a run before doing more. Changing the judge resets the baselines, so it would sit behind its own flag. Paid runs would still need your approval for each batch.

**File-load report** ([Add chosen facts to the file-load report](#local_4514e803-fed9-427a-96d5-ea65e92ed8bc)):

Three things from its report you should know:

All three sessions I started are finished and idle, and each reports its task done. What's left is two unmerged branches and a few follow-ups that are your call. Nothing has been pushed anywhere.

- **74c1335d8f:** the chat panel opens at 429 px.

- **c9d96d2090:** the fit, mesh and file facts in the file-load report.
- **c65cad6dfb:** the file-loaded skill rewrite. It's a separate commit, so you can drop it and keep the facts.

**Left to decide:**
1. **Merge the test-harness branches.**
   - `refs/heads/claude/claude-cli-backend` (`ddc771948a`) is the subscription backend.
   - `refs/heads/claude/opus-recorded-reads` sits on top of it. `24303e3a67` adds recorded answers for two reads Opus makes that the recording lacked. `e7b7db2c69` changes the app's `intent_update` tool description so the agent records only a purpose the person actually stated. That second commit is a product change, not just test code.
   - Both branch off before the facts commits, but a dry-run merge into `jusprin-newui` goes through without conflicts.
2. **Re-record the requests after merging.** The re-recorded `requests.json` on that branch came from an app build without the new report facts or the skill rewrite. Prompt runs would test the old file-load report until it's recorded again.
3. **Make a subscription baseline.** You said "not yet". Once the requests are re-recorded, one full run of all 24 cases would give results that later prompt changes can be compared against.
4. **Fix a runner bug.** The runner answers reads whose arguments the app would refuse. [Record the reads Opus makes that the recording lacks](#local_bdc36c1e-181d-4c20-9e41-2c7ae71dfaa6) left a card for a session to fix it, waiting for you to start it.
5. **Add the backend to the printer suite.** `tests/printer_prompt` doesn't have the subscription backend. Its runner shares no code with the project suite's, so that would be separate work.
6. **Settle the Kobra 3 question.** OrcaSlicer reads the Kobra 3 profile's excluded areas in a way that covers the whole bed. So the report says every object on a Kobra 3 is off the bed, even though the app shows no error. Whether slicing is actually refused on that printer is unverified.
7. **Handle the latest `print-this-no-purpose` result.** After the `intent_update` change, Opus no longer records a guessed purpose. The case still passes only 1 of 3, because two replies asked two questions where the case allows one.
8. **Two local notes.**

model asked for (`{"accepted": true}`), and let it run on: it wandered for 10

## What keeps it faithful to the app

- **The system prompt** comes from the page's own source, through
  `tests/printer_prompt/render_prompt.mjs` (`"kind": "project"`) and the page's
  esbuild. This needs node and the AgentUI npm install. `--prompt-rev REV`
  renders it as it was at a git revision, 6b4b8b6188 or later (the commit
  that moved the prompt from C++ to the page, unchanged).
- **`project_tools.json`** is the tool list the app sends in the project chat
  with nothing attached. `test_openai_responses_agent.cpp` fails when it
  drifts from the registry. Regenerate it with
  `JUSPRIN_UPDATE_PROJECT_TOOLS=1 agent_bridge_tests '[project]'`.
- **Everything else in the request** is the app's: `requests.json`, recorded
  by the shell harness from `script.json`:

  request that carries a chip's message or first shows a slice's new
  warnings, the slice-failed skill on the request that first shows a
  refused or failed slice, the setup skill on the request that first
  carries a recorded or changed purpose or a setup change under one, and
  the live results of this turn's calls with the
  workspace block `AgentHost::continue_after_tool` adds. Arguments that need
  ids take them from the real previous result (`{{result/sessionId}}`) or the
  project (`{{workspace/activePlateId}}`). For each request it keeps, the
  harness checks the tools equal `project_tools.json` and the instructions
  equal `projectInstructions.fixture.txt`, then leaves both out of the file;
  the runner puts the rendered prompt and `project_tools.json` back. The
  script's `answers` list names the reads recorded at every point.
  `test_openai_responses_agent.cpp` also checks every recorded result and
  answer against its tool's output schema.
- **Answered reads** are added as the app continues a turn: the model's own
  output items, then a result for every call under its call id, in the order
  the calls were written. Each answer carries the action id and workspace
  block of the recorded call. A point's `once` (in `requests.json`) counts
  the last items of its request that the app sends on that request alone,
  a skill's text and, for the file-loaded skill, its picture; the runner
  drops them before it answers
  a read, as the app does.
- **Skills** (`AgentUI/src/skills/*/SKILL.md`) reach the model only in the
  recorded requests: the app adds one to the request where its event first
  reaches the model, as that request's last item. The recorder checks that a
  point the script marks `"skill": "<name>"` ends with that skill (after the
  plate's picture for `file-loaded`), that no other point
  carries a skill or a picture, so an import's point carries the
  file-loaded skill alone, and that the next request of the same turn (the
  first answered read) has none.
  A skill edit therefore needs a new recording, unlike a prompt edit.

What is written by hand is only what a model or a person would have said: the
person's words, the scripted calls, and two assistant replies (the summary
after the prepare turn and the first message about an opened file). The
scripted calls carry the replay form the app uses (`call_id`, `name`,
`arguments`); a live model's own item id, status and reasoning items within a
turn are not reproducible. Nothing checks that `requests.json` stays current:
record it again when a tool's results, the fixture or the request shape
change. It was recorded with the change that moved the workspace snapshot
and the issue context into tagged blocks of their own, the commit after
